proof:
Every halfspace in $U$ through $p=\pi_U(y_*)$ lifts to an ambient halfspace through $y_*$. Its pushforward mass is at least $A$, and the selected normals give caps of mass exactly $A$. A containing halfspace contains its parallel through-point halfspace, so the projected raw depth of $p$ is $A$. At any $z\in U$, the balance gives $u_i\cdot(z-p)\ge0$ for some $i$. The halfspace $u_i\cdot w\ge u_i\cdot z$ contains $z$ and is contained in the halfspace $u_i\cdot w\ge u_i\cdot p$ of mass $A$. This bounds every projected candidate, including points outside the support.

Fubini gives the slice formula and total mass $|K|$. The support is the compact convex body $\pi_U(K)$ because projection takes the interior of $K$ onto the interior of $\pi_U(K)$. For the latter assertion, take an interior point of $K$ and extend the segment from its projection to any given point of $\operatorname{int}\pi_U(K)$ slightly past that point in $\pi_U(K)$. Interpolating the interior point with a preimage of the far endpoint gives an interior preimage of the given point. This also shows positivity of the slice volume there, while boundedness follows by enclosing $K$ in a ball. For $r<d$, Minkowski interpolation of the parallel slices and Brunn–Minkowski show concavity of the positive slice-volume power $1/(d-r)$ wherever the two slices have positive volume. This proves log-concavity, with the zero-density cases immediate, and interior continuity. When $r=d$ the indicator supplies the same properties.

For existence of the balance, every deepest point is interior. An interior inball gives positive depth at its center, whereas at a boundary point a supporting halfspace meets $K$ only in a Lebesgue-null plane. Through-point cap masses are jointly continuous in unit normal and mark by dominated convergence off the limiting hyperplane. Hence the active set at $y_*$ is nonempty and compact. If its convex hull omits zero, strict separation gives a vector $v$ whose scalar products with the active normals are uniformly positive. On an open neighborhood of the active normals, these scalar products are still bounded below by a positive constant. Moving the mark a small distance along $-v$ increases every cap in that neighborhood by a uniform positive multiple of the distance, from the added slabs inside an inball about $y_*$. On the remaining compact set of normals the old masses have a uniform positive gap above $A$, which persists for a small move by joint continuity. This contradicts maximality. Carathéodory gives a finite balance, and deleting zero coefficients makes it positive. If a balanced family has rank one, it contains both unit normals in its line. Their caps have mass $A$ and partition $K$ up to a null hyperplane. Thus $A=|K|/2$. Any other pair of opposite caps each have mass at least $A$ and sum to $|K|$, so every direction is active.
statement:
Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a full-dimensional compact convex body, and let $y_*$ attain its maximum raw ordinary closed-halfspace depth $A$. A unit normal $u$ is active at $y_*$ if the cap $u\cdot(x-y_*)\ge0$ in $K$ has volume $A$. Suppose that a finite active family $u_i$ admits a positive balance $\sum_i\lambda_i u_i=0$, with all $\lambda_i>0$. Let $U=\operatorname{span}\{u_i\}$ have dimension $r$, and let $\pi_U$ be orthogonal projection onto $U$. The pushforward of the volume of $K$ to $U$ has raw maximum closed-halfspace depth exactly $A$, attained at $\pi_U(y_*)$. Its density at $z\in\pi_U(K)$ is the perpendicular slice volume $\mathcal H^{d-r}(K\cap(z+U^\perp))$ for $r<d$, and is the indicator of $K$ when $r=d$. This density is bounded and log-concave, positive and continuous in the interior of its compact full-dimensional support.

At any such $y_*$ the full set of active unit normals has a finite positively balanced subfamily. If it has a balanced subfamily of rank one, then $A=|K|/2$ and all unit normals are active. Hence for $d>1$ the complete active span cannot have rank one.
title: Projection to a balanced active normal span preserves maximum depth
